lessons.title: The Four Principles
body: Bioethics is the study of moral questions raised by medicine and the life sciences. The most widely taught framework is called principlism, set out by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in their book Principles of Biomedical Ethics, first published in 1979. It names four principles that clinicians, researchers and policymakers can use to reason through problems.

Autonomy is respect for the self-determination of a person who has the capacity to decide. A competent patient may accept or refuse treatment even when a doctor disagrees. Beneficence is the duty to act for the patient's benefit, such as treating illness or relieving pain. Non-maleficence, often summarized in the Latin phrase primum non nocere, means avoiding harm, or at least not causing harm that outweighs benefit. Justice concerns fairness in how benefits, burdens and risks are distributed, such as who receives a scarce resource.

The principles are prima facie, which means each one binds unless it conflicts with another that is weightier in the situation. That is why they are a toolkit and not a formula. Suppose a competent adult with a treatable infection refuses antibiotics. Beneficence and non-maleficence point toward treating, but autonomy points toward respecting refusal. In most legal systems and in professional ethics, a capable adult's informed refusal prevails, although the clinician keeps explaining, exploring reasons and offering alternatives.

Common traps: treating autonomy as absolute (it is limited, for example, when others would be harmed or when capacity is lacking) and assuming that the principles always give one answer. Careful ethical reasoning identifies which principles are in tension, gathers the facts, hears the patient's values, and gives reasons that others could examine.

lessons.title: Informed Consent and Capacity
body: Informed consent is more than a signature. It is a process in which a clinician gives a patient the information needed to decide, the patient has the capacity to decide, and the choice is voluntary. The legal roots are old. In Schloendorff v. Society of New York Hospital (New York, 1914), Judge Cardozo wrote that every adult of sound mind has a right to determine what is done with his own body, and that surgery without consent is an assault. The phrase informed consent itself became common after a 1957 California case, Salgo v. Leland Stanford Jr. University Board of Trustees.

What must be disclosed? Courts split. Under the older professional standard, the doctor discloses what a reasonable physician would disclose. Under the patient-oriented standard, adopted in Canterbury v. Spence (D.C. Circuit, 1972), the doctor must disclose the risks a reasonable patient would consider material to the decision. Many US states follow each approach. Typical disclosures cover the diagnosis, the nature and purpose of the proposed treatment, its main risks and benefits, reasonable alternatives (including no treatment), and the expected outcome.

Capacity is decision-specific and is assessed by clinicians, not decided by a diagnosis or by age alone. Clinicians commonly look for four abilities: understanding the information, appreciating how it applies to oneself, reasoning about options, and expressing a stable choice. A patient with dementia may have capacity for one simple decision but not for a complex one. Disagreeing with the doctor is not evidence of incapacity.

There are exceptions. In a true emergency, when a patient cannot consent and delay threatens life or serious harm, treatment is generally allowed under implied consent. For patients lacking capacity, a surrogate decides, ideally using substituted judgment (what the patient would have wanted) and otherwise the patient's best interests. Minors are usually represented by parents, though many places allow minors to consent for certain services, and adolescents are asked for assent.

A worked example: a patient who is conscious, understands that declining a blood transfusion may be fatal, and says so consistently has capacity and may refuse, even if the clinician considers refusal unwise.

lessons.title: Confidentiality and Its Limits
body: Patients disclose embarrassing and frightening facts to clinicians because they expect confidentiality. Without that expectation people might hide symptoms, avoid care or lie, which harms both them and public health. Confidentiality is therefore both a duty owed to the individual and a condition for good medicine. Its roots reach back to the Hippocratic tradition, and modern codes of medical ethics repeat it.

In the United States the HIPAA Privacy Rule, issued under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, regulates how covered entities such as health plans and providers may use and disclose protected health information. In broad terms it permits sharing for treatment, payment and health care operations, requires patient authorization for many other uses, and lets patients see their records. Other countries have comparable privacy laws, and some US states add stronger protections for categories such as mental health or reproductive health.

Confidentiality is not absolute. Common exceptions include legally required reports of certain infectious diseases to public health authorities, gunshot wounds in many states, and suspected abuse of a child or vulnerable adult by mandated reporters. A famous case is Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (California Supreme Court, 1976). A patient told a psychologist that he intended to kill a woman and then did. The court held that when a therapist determines, or under professional standards should determine, that a patient presents a serious danger of violence to another, the therapist has a duty to use reasonable care to protect the intended victim. States have since adopted varied versions of this duty, some as a duty to warn, some as a duty to protect, and some not at all.

A useful test is proportionality: disclose only the minimum necessary, to the proper person, for a recognized, serious reason, and tell the patient where possible. Example: a teen asks a clinic for confidential contraception. Rules vary by state, but the clinician should explain the limits of confidentiality at the start so the teen can decide what to share.

lessons.title: Mental Health, Capacity and Autonomy
body: Mental illness raises a hard question: respect for autonomy assumes a person can make decisions, yet some conditions affect judgment, insight or mood. The key point is that a psychiatric diagnosis is not the same as lacking capacity. Many people with depression, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder have capacity for most decisions, and clinicians must assess capacity for the specific decision at hand.

Society also permits limited involuntary psychiatric care. Standards differ by state, but typical criteria require a mental disorder together with danger to self, danger to others, or in some places grave disability, meaning an inability to meet basic needs such as food and shelter. Commitment usually requires procedural protections: an evaluation, a time limit, a hearing and legal representation. In O'Connor v. Donaldson (US Supreme Court, 1975), the Court held that a state cannot constitutionally confine a non-dangerous person who is capable of surviving safely in freedom, simply because he is mentally ill. Courts have also required due process before involuntary treatment with medication in many settings.

Two principles guide the balance. The first is least restrictive alternative: if a safe option exists that restricts liberty less than hospitalization, such as outpatient treatment, it should be preferred. The second is that decisions made during illness may differ from a person's long-term values. Psychiatric advance directives let a person write down in a time of wellness how they would like to be treated in a later crisis, which supports autonomy across time.

The ethical tension is real in both directions. Over-intervening can strip dignity and discourage people from seeking help. Under-intervening can leave a person to suffer or die when treatment could restore their ability to choose. Careful clinicians ask whether the disorder is impairing the specific decision, whether less restrictive options exist, and whether the person's own past wishes can guide care.

Example: a person with severe depression who refuses food and says they do not deserve to live may lack the capacity to refuse treatment, but a person with a stable, different belief about medication who shows a clear understanding and consistent reasoning is entitled to decline.

lessons.title: Nuremberg and the Birth of Research Ethics
body: During the Second World War, physicians in Nazi Germany and in the camps it ran carried out cruel experiments on prisoners, who could not refuse. After the war, the United States held trials at Nuremberg. The Doctors' Trial (1946 to 1947) tried 23 defendants, mostly physicians and officials, and many were convicted of war crimes and crimes against humanity; several were sentenced to death. In the judgment, the judges set out ten principles for permissible human experimentation. These are known as the Nuremberg Code.

The first and most famous principle states that the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. Consent must be given by a person with legal capacity, free of force, fraud or coercion, and with enough knowledge of the experiment to make an informed decision. Other principles require that the experiment aim to produce useful results unobtainable by other means, that it be based on prior animal studies, avoid unnecessary suffering, not risk death or disabling injury except perhaps when the researchers also serve as subjects, and that the subject be free to end the experiment at any time. The risk must never exceed the humanitarian importance of the problem.

The Code was not itself law and was written in response to a specific set of crimes, but it shaped later documents. In 1964 the World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Helsinki, a statement of ethical principles for medical research that has been revised several times. Unlike Nuremberg, it was written by physicians for physicians, and it added ideas such as independent review of research protocols.

Why this matters: the Code established that scientific benefit does not by itself justify using a person as a means. A common mistake is to assume that research abuses were confined to one country or period. The next lessons show that the United States had its own, and that consent rules were often ignored even after Nuremberg.

lessons.title: Tuskegee and the Belmont Report
body: In 1932 the US Public Health Service began a study in Macon County, Alabama, to observe the natural course of untreated syphilis. About 600 Black men took part, roughly 400 with syphilis and about 200 without as a comparison group. The men were told they were being treated for bad blood and were given free meals, medical exams and burial insurance. They were never told they had syphilis in a way they could understand, and the study did not aim to treat it.

When penicillin became the standard, effective treatment for syphilis in the 1940s, the men were not offered it, and officials took steps to keep them from getting treatment elsewhere. The study ran for forty years. It ended in 1972 after a former Public Health Service employee, Peter Buxtun, who had raised concerns internally, told a reporter, and the Associated Press story brought public outrage. Many participants had died of syphilis or related complications, and some of their wives and children had been infected.

The response reshaped US research rules. Congress passed the National Research Act of 1974, which required institutional review boards for federally funded research and created a national commission. The commission produced the Belmont Report in 1979, which names three principles: respect for persons (including informed consent and protection of those with diminished autonomy), beneficence (maximizing benefits and minimizing harms), and justice (fair selection of research subjects, so that burdens do not fall on one group while benefits go to another). In 1997 President Clinton formally apologized to the survivors and their families.

The lasting lessons are about consent, honesty and justice, and also about trust. The study is often cited as one reason that some Black Americans distrust medical institutions, and building trust requires transparent practices. A common error is to say the men were infected by the government. Historians' accounts are that they already had the disease, but they were deceived and denied known treatment.

lessons.title: Henrietta Lacks and the Ownership of Cells
body: In 1951, Henrietta Lacks, a Black woman from Baltimore, was treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital. During her care, samples of her tumor were taken and given to a researcher. Her cells proved unusually able to grow and divide in the laboratory, which at the time was a major challenge, and became the first immortal human cell line. Called HeLa, it was used in countless studies, including work on the polio vaccine, cancer, viruses and gene mapping. Henrietta Lacks died in 1951, and her family did not know of the cell line for years.

At the time, consent for research use of leftover tissue was not required as it is for experiments today, so there was no clear legal wrong. But the story highlights ethical issues. She was not asked, her family was not told, and her identity and later her genome became public in ways the family had not agreed to. In 2013, researchers published the HeLa genome, and after the family objected, the National Institutes of Health reached an agreement with the family that gives them a say in who can access the genomic data.

A related legal case is Moore v. Regents of the University of California (California Supreme Court, 1990). A patient's cells were used by doctors to develop a profitable cell line. The court said that the doctors had a duty to disclose their research and financial interests, but it did not accept that the patient had a property right in cells removed from his body.

Debates continue about whether donors should control uses of tissue, share in profits, or receive recognition. The revised Common Rule, the US federal policy on human subjects research, took effect in 2018 and changed rules about consent for secondary research with biospecimens. Careful reasoning separates two questions: what the law required at the time, and what ethics suggests we should do now.

lessons.title: How Research Is Reviewed Today
body: Modern research ethics turns the lessons of Nuremberg, Tuskegee and others into routine procedures. In the United States, most federally funded human research follows the Common Rule (45 CFR part 46), and research on drugs and devices follows Food and Drug Administration regulations. Before a study begins, an institutional review board (IRB), a committee that includes scientists and non-scientists, reviews the protocol. It asks whether risks are reasonable relative to benefits, whether participants are selected fairly, whether consent is properly obtained and documented, whether privacy is protected, and whether the study is safe as it proceeds.

Informed consent in research must explain the purpose, procedures, risks, potential benefits, alternatives and the right to withdraw without penalty. Consent forms are meant to be understandable, though studies show that long, technical forms can obscure risk. Extra protections apply to vulnerable groups, including children, prisoners, pregnant people and those with cognitive impairment, because they may be more easily coerced or less able to protect their interests.

A central concept is clinical equipoise, the idea that a randomized trial is ethical when there is genuine uncertainty in the expert community about which treatment is better. If a treatment is already known to be effective, giving some participants a placebo may be unethical, and the control group should receive the best standard therapy. Large trials also use data and safety monitoring boards, which can stop a study early if one arm shows clear harm or clear benefit.

Example: researchers propose a trial of a new blood pressure drug against placebo in people with severe hypertension. Because effective treatments exist, an IRB is likely to require that the comparison be against standard therapy, not placebo alone.
Common traps: confusing therapeutic misconception with consent, where participants believe the trial is designed to treat them individually, and thinking IRB approval ends ethical responsibility.

lessons.title: Public Health versus Individual Liberty
body: Public health aims to protect and improve the health of populations. Its tools include vaccination programs, quarantine and isolation, reporting of diseases, sanitation rules and health education. Many of these ask individuals to accept limits for the good of others. The ethical question is when such limits are justified.

An influential idea is John Stuart Mill's harm principle: society may limit a person's liberty to prevent harm to others, but not simply for the person's own good. Infectious disease fits the harm principle clearly because one person's infection can harm others. In the United States, the leading case is Jacobson v. Massachusetts (US Supreme Court, 1905), which upheld a local law requiring smallpox vaccination or a modest fine, holding that states may use their police power to enact reasonable regulations to protect public health. The Court noted limits: measures must be reasonable and not arbitrary or oppressive. The decision is still cited, though modern courts also apply later doctrines on individual rights and religious freedom.

Ethicists often propose conditions for justified restrictions: there is a real public health threat, the measure is likely to be effective, it is necessary, it is the least restrictive effective option, its burdens are proportionate to the benefits, it is applied fairly, and the public is told the reasons. Quarantine (separating healthy people who may have been exposed) and isolation (separating people who are sick) are examples.

The debate over vaccine mandates shows reasonable disagreement. Supporters point to community protection and to people who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons. Opponents emphasize bodily integrity, personal or religious conviction, and doubts about government coercion. Policies differ widely: many US states allow school vaccination exemptions of various kinds, while others restrict them. Teaching the matter fairly means separating what the law requires, which varies by place, from the values at issue.

lessons.title: Organ Donation and Allocation
body: For many people with organ failure, a transplant is the best or only treatment, but there are far fewer donated organs than patients who need them. That scarcity creates two ethical problems: how to obtain organs, and how to distribute them fairly.

On obtaining organs, there are two main legal models. In an opt-in system, which the United States uses, a person must register agreement to donate, or family members agree on their behalf. In an opt-out system, sometimes called presumed consent, a person is presumed to be a donor unless they register an objection. Several European countries use opt-out laws, and in practice families are often still consulted. The evidence on whether opt-out increases donation is mixed, because infrastructure and family consent practices also matter.

The National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 made it illegal in the United States to buy or sell human organs for valuable consideration. Supporters of the ban stress risks of exploitation of the poor and commodification of the body. Critics argue regulated payment could save lives and respect autonomy, while noting that most countries other than Iran ban organ sales.

Donation after death rests on the dead donor rule: vital organs may be taken only from a person who is dead, and the person must not be killed by procurement. Death can be determined by irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function, or by irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, which is the basis of the Uniform Determination of Death Act of 1981. Living donors can give a kidney or part of a liver, which requires careful consent to avoid pressure from family.

Allocation systems in the United States are overseen under federal law and use medical criteria, not social worth. Factors typically include blood type compatibility, medical urgency, the likelihood of benefit, time waiting and geography, with details that differ by organ and change over time. A liver candidate, for example, is ranked largely by a score of how sick the patient is. Ethical debates include whether to give priority to younger patients, whether alcohol-related liver disease should reduce priority, and how to balance urgency against expected benefit.

lessons.title: Genetic Screening, Testing and CRISPR
body: Genetic technologies raise ethical questions because genetic information is personal, predictive and shared with relatives. Several different practices need to be kept apart.

Screening looks at populations to find people who may be at risk. Newborn screening, which tests a few drops of blood from nearly every baby in many countries, detects conditions such as phenylketonuria where early treatment prevents harm. Prenatal screening, including tests of cell-free DNA in the pregnant person's blood, estimates the chance of certain chromosome conditions, and diagnostic tests confirm. Carrier screening checks for recessive gene variants in prospective parents. Preimplantation genetic testing examines embryos made by in vitro fertilization. Ethical questions include informed choice, avoiding pressure, the information that may be found unexpectedly, and what disability-rights advocates call the expressive message that screening sends about the value of lives with disabilities.

Privacy and fairness are also in play. In the United States, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 bars health insurers and employers from discriminating on the basis of genetic information, but it does not cover life, disability or long-term care insurance.

Gene editing is a further step. CRISPR-Cas9, adapted from a bacterial defense system and developed by researchers including Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier, who shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, lets scientists cut DNA at chosen locations. Somatic editing changes cells in one person and is not inherited; in 2023 regulators in the United Kingdom and the United States approved the first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease. Germline editing changes embryos, eggs or sperm, so the change could be passed down to future generations who cannot consent. In 2018, the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced the birth of gene-edited twins; the work was widely condemned, and he was later sentenced to prison in China.

Fair debate asks whether safety, consent, enhancement versus therapy, and equity of access can be satisfied. Some argue that germline editing to prevent serious disease could someday be acceptable under strict oversight. Others argue for a long pause or a ban because of safety, inequality and the risk of eugenic thinking.

lessons.title: Reproductive Ethics Presented Fairly
body: Reproductive ethics includes some of the most contested questions in society. This lesson separates the law, which is a matter of fact, from the arguments, where thoughtful people disagree.

The law in the United States: in Roe v. Wade (1973) and Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), the Supreme Court recognized a constitutional right to abortion before viability. In Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022), the Court overruled Roe and Casey, holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion and that the matter returns to the states and their legislatures. As a result, laws vary substantially by state and continue to change, so the legal position in any given place should be checked directly. Other countries differ widely.

The main arguments are better understood than caricatured. One view holds that a human life with moral worth begins at conception or very early, so abortion wrongs a human being, and that society should protect that being, perhaps with exceptions for the mother's life or other grave situations. A second view holds that a pregnant person has the right to control her own body, that forcing continuation of pregnancy imposes severe burdens, and that access to safe abortion protects health and equality. A third family of views is gradualist: moral status increases over time, perhaps tied to viability or sentience, so early abortion is more permissible than late abortion. Disagreements concern moral status of the embryo and fetus, the weight of bodily autonomy, and the role of law as against conscience.

Assisted reproduction raises related questions. In vitro fertilization often produces more embryos than are used, so there are questions about storing, donating, researching on or discarding embryos, which depend on one's view of embryo status. Surrogacy raises questions about exploitation, payment and parental rights, and laws differ greatly. Prenatal testing raises questions about selection.
Good ethical reasoning here identifies the premise at the root of a disagreement, such as moral status or bodily autonomy, and accepts that reasonable people may weigh them differently.

lessons.title: End-of-Life Decisions
body: Medicine can often prolong life in ways that may not match what a patient values. End-of-life ethics asks who decides, on what basis, and where the lines fall.

Two cases shaped US law. Karen Ann Quinlan, aged 21, lost consciousness in 1975 and entered a persistent vegetative state. Her parents asked that her ventilator be removed. In In re Quinlan (New Jersey Supreme Court, 1976), the court allowed it, reasoning that her right of privacy included a right to decline treatment that could be exercised by her guardian, and the case encouraged hospital ethics committees. After the ventilator was removed she kept breathing and lived for about nine more years. In Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health (US Supreme Court, 1990), the Court assumed that a competent person has a constitutionally protected liberty interest in refusing life-sustaining treatment, including artificial nutrition and hydration, but held that a state may require clear and convincing evidence of an incompetent patient's wishes. Cruzan led to wider use of advance directives such as living wills and health care proxies, and to the federal Patient Self-Determination Act of 1990.

Important distinctions include withholding versus withdrawing treatment (most ethicists see them as morally equivalent, since a patient may refuse treatment either way), letting die versus actively causing death, and the doctrine of double effect, which holds that giving needed pain relief that may incidentally hasten death can be permissible if the intent is to relieve suffering.

Assisted dying is more contested. In Washington v. Glucksberg and Vacco v. Quill (1997), the Supreme Court held that there is no constitutional right to assisted suicide but that states may permit or prohibit it. Oregon's Death with Dignity Act, approved by voters in 1994 and in effect from 1997, permits eligible terminally ill adults to obtain medication they take themselves; several other US states and countries have since passed laws of varying scope, and some countries permit clinician-administered euthanasia. As of this writing, laws are changing, so check the current position.

The arguments should be held fairly. Supporters stress autonomy, compassion and relief of suffering. Opponents stress the sanctity of life, the integrity of the medical profession as healers, risks to vulnerable people such as those with disabilities or without good care, and the possibility of subtle pressure. Palliative care is valued by most sides as a way to reduce suffering.

lessons.title: Scarcity, Triage and Crisis Standards
body: In a crisis such as a pandemic surge or disaster, demand for ventilators, beds or staff may exceed supply. Triage is the practice of prioritizing patients under scarcity. The word comes from French, and the practice was developed on battlefields. Hospitals and governments write crisis standards of care in advance so that decisions are not left to a clinician's moment-by-moment judgment.

Commonly proposed ethical aims include saving the most lives, giving priority to those who can benefit most, treating people equally, and keeping decisions transparent and open to appeal. Many plans rate the short-term likelihood of survival, sometimes using organ failure scores. Plans often reject first come, first served as the sole criterion, because it favors those who can reach hospitals fastest, and reject social worth, such as occupation or wealth, as a basis for ranking, except that giving priority to health care workers is sometimes defended as instrumental, so that they can keep treating others.

A central concern is disability discrimination. If a plan excludes people with disabilities from treatment because of assumptions about quality of life, it may break laws such as the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. Rules should rest on evidence of short-term benefit, not on stereotypes or on age alone. Some plans also use ongoing reassessment, in which patients who do not improve may lose a ventilator to someone with better odds, which is ethically distressing and requires clear policy and explanation.

Process matters: separating triage decisions from treating clinicians reduces moral distress and bias, and palliative care should always be offered to those who do not receive the scarce treatment. The principle of non-abandonment says that even when a treatment is not available, care continues.

Example: two patients need the last ventilator. One has a good short-term prognosis, and one has a poorer prognosis from a different illness. A plan based on short-term survival would favor the first, whereas a plan based only on age or disability status would be open to serious criticism.

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine
body: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems that find patterns in data are used in medicine to read images, predict deterioration, summarize records and draft messages. As of this writing, this field is changing quickly, and rules are still developing. The ethical questions apply the older principles to a new setting.

Accuracy and safety come first. A model may perform well in the hospital where it was built and poorly in another with different patients, equipment or practice. It can also drift as practice changes. Evidence from properly designed studies is therefore more important than a company's claims. In the United States, some AI software is regulated by the Food and Drug Administration as a medical device, and in the European Union broader AI rules classify many medical uses as high risk.

Bias and justice: a model learns from past data, which may reflect past inequities. A widely cited 2019 study in the journal Science reported that a commercial algorithm used health care costs as a proxy for health needs, and because less money was spent on Black patients with the same level of illness, it underestimated their needs. The lesson is that the choice of what to predict, and the data used, can carry bias.

Transparency and accountability: many models are hard to interpret. Clinicians and patients may reasonably ask how a recommendation was produced, and the clinician remains responsible for the care given. Automation bias is the tendency to over-trust a machine's output, and deskilling is the risk that clinicians lose skills they stop using.

Consent and privacy: patients may deserve to know when AI contributes to their care, and training models on records raises questions of consent and data protection. Chatbots that give health advice can be confidently wrong.

A useful approach is to treat AI as a tool inside a system of human responsibility: test it locally, monitor it for errors and unequal performance, keep a human who can override it, and be honest with patients about its role.

questions.prompt: Which set correctly names the four principles in the Beauchamp and Childress framework?
choices: Justice, veracity, fidelity and institutional trust
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice
Autonomy, loyalty, honesty and professional duty
Beneficence, efficiency, utility and public benefit

questions.prompt: What does it mean to call the principles prima facie?
choices: Each binds unless it conflicts with a weightier principle in the situation
Each must be applied in a fixed order of rank in every single case, with autonomy always first
Each applies only to physicians and never to researchers or nurses
Each is only a suggestion with no real moral weight in medicine

questions.prompt: A capable adult declines a treatable infection's antibiotics after a full discussion. Which principle most directly supports respecting the refusal?
choices: Beneficence
Non-maleficence
Justice
Autonomy

questions.prompt: A hospital must decide how to distribute a limited number of ICU beds during a surge. A committee proposes giving priority by medical need and likelihood of benefit rather than social status. Which principle is the committee mainly applying, and what does it require?
choices: Non-maleficence, because no patient should ever be denied a bed under any circumstance
Beneficence, because the hospital must maximize its own financial return from each bed
Justice, because scarce benefits should be distributed by fair criteria that are relevant to need and outcome
Autonomy, because each patient must be allowed to choose which intensive care bed that they will occupy during the surge

questions.prompt: In Schloendorff v. Society of New York Hospital (1914), the court recognized that:
choices: consent forms are required only for experimental treatments in hospitals
patients lose the right to refuse once they have entered a hospital
an adult of sound mind has a right to decide what is done to his own body
physicians may operate whenever they think surgery is medically best

questions.prompt: Canterbury v. Spence (D.C. Cir. 1972) is associated with which disclosure standard?
choices: The professional standard, based on what other physicians customarily tell patients
The subjective standard, based on each patient's private personal wishes alone
The emergency standard, based on what is necessary to save a life
The reasonable patient standard, based on risks material to a patient's decision

questions.prompt: Which feature of capacity is most accurate?
choices: It is decision-specific and can be present for one decision but not another
It is the same as a psychiatric diagnosis and is determined by a court only
It is determined by age, and every adult has full capacity for all choices
It is lost whenever a patient disagrees with the recommendation of a doctor

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old woman with a bleeding gastric ulcer is alert, understands that refusing a transfusion may kill her, explains that it conflicts with her religious faith, and has said the same for years. Which is the most ethically and legally appropriate response?
choices: Delay all care until a court has decided that she no longer has decision-making capacity
Respect her informed refusal while offering non-blood alternatives and continuing to discuss
Transfuse anyway because preserving life always outweighs the religious beliefs of a patient
Ask her adult child to override her decision since she is seriously ill and in danger

questions.prompt: An unconscious trauma patient arrives bleeding heavily with no family present. Treatment is begun without a signed form. Which doctrine justifies this?
choices: Therapeutic privilege
Assent of the patient
Implied consent in an emergency
Substituted judgment by a court

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the role of confidentiality in medicine?
choices: It protects doctors from being asked questions about the patients they treat
It is an absolute duty that has no exceptions of any kind in any situation
It applies only to records on paper and not to spoken conversations
It encourages honest disclosure, which supports both individual care and public health

questions.prompt: Which is a common legal exception to confidentiality in many places?
choices: Posting a patient's diagnosis to a hospital newsletter
Telling the neighbors of a patient about the treatment
Mandated reporting of suspected child abuse
Sharing records with an employer who asks about a worker

questions.prompt: In Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (Cal. 1976), the court held that a therapist who determines a patient is a serious danger to another person must:
choices: report the patient to an employer so that the patient can be fired
use reasonable care to protect the intended victim
wait for the patient to commit a violent act before taking any steps
keep confidence in all cases because therapy depends on secrecy

questions.prompt: A 16-year-old tells a clinic physician she is sexually active and wants contraception and asks that her parents not be told. Local law permits minors to consent to contraception. What is the best approach?
choices: Provide care, explain confidentiality and its limits, and encourage her to involve a trusted adult
Refuse care until a parent has come to the clinic and signed a form saying that they agree with the request
Call her parents right away because all information about minors belongs to parents
Provide care and promise complete secrecy in every circumstance, even if she later reports abuse by an adult

questions.prompt: Which statement about psychiatric diagnosis and capacity is most accurate?
choices: A diagnosis does not by itself mean a person lacks capacity for a decision
Anyone who has a diagnosis of mental illness automatically lacks capacity
Capacity is judged only by the family of the patient and never by clinicians
Capacity is the same for every decision and does not vary with a situation

questions.prompt: Which of these is a typical legal criterion for involuntary commitment in many US states?
choices: A request by an employer or landlord to remove the person
A mental disorder together with danger to self or others
A disagreement with the recommendation of a treating physician
Any history of previous contact with mental health services

questions.prompt: What did the Supreme Court hold in O'Connor v. Donaldson (1975)?
choices: A person who has been confined may never again be treated with any medication
A state must always provide free housing for every person with mental illness
A state may not confine a non-dangerous person who can live safely in freedom simply because of mental illness
A state may confine any person with a mental illness if relatives request it

questions.prompt: A man with schizophrenia, stable on medication, writes a psychiatric advance directive during remission stating which treatments he accepts in a future relapse. During a later relapse he refuses admission. Which ethical idea best supports giving weight to his directive?
choices: Justice, since all people with mental illness must receive an identical treatment plan
Non-maleficence, since a written document can never contain any ethical risk at all
Beneficence, since a doctor's judgment in the moment must always override any statements that the patient made earlier in life
Autonomy extended across time, since the directive reflects his considered values while well

questions.prompt: What is the first principle of the Nuremberg Code?
choices: Subjects must be paid a fair wage for taking part in experiments
The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential
Experiments must be approved in advance by the government of the country where they are done
Research may proceed whenever the results are valuable to society

questions.prompt: The Nuremberg Code arose from which event?
choices: The Doctors' Trial held after the Second World War
A congressional hearing on pharmaceutical advertising in the 1960s
The founding of the World Health Organization in 1948 in Geneva
A court ruling on the safety of the first polio vaccine trials

questions.prompt: How does the Declaration of Helsinki (1964) differ from the Nuremberg Code?
choices: It was written by a criminal court as part of a judgment against a group of physicians
It abolished the need for subjects to give consent to research studies
It applies only to experiments that are carried out on animals
It was written by the medical profession and added independent review of research protocols

questions.prompt: A researcher argues that a dangerous experiment on prisoners is justified because the knowledge gained would save thousands of lives. Under the Nuremberg Code, what is the best response?
choices: The experiment is acceptable if a prison official gives permission for the prisoners
The experiment is acceptable provided that no subject dies before it is complete
Benefit to society cannot replace voluntary informed consent of each subject

questions.prompt: What was the central ethical failure of the Tuskegee study after penicillin became standard for syphilis?

The study had been stopped before enough data had been collected
Participants were not offered effective treatment and were not told the truth
Participants received much more medicine than was safe at each of their regular visits

questions.prompt: Which three principles are named in the Belmont Report (1979)?
choices: Autonomy, loyalty and the collective public interest of the whole society
Honesty, veracity and the avoidance of all risk
Consent, secrecy and scientific freedom for scientists
Respect for persons, beneficence and justice

A complete ban on all medical research that involves human volunteers in the country
Payment of every research participant by the federal government

questions.prompt: A committee reviewing a trial notices that all participants are drawn from one low-income community, while the likely beneficiaries are wealthy patients elsewhere. Which Belmont principle is most directly implicated?

Justice, because burdens and benefits should be fairly distributed in selecting subjects

Respect for persons, because low-income people are unable to give consent in any way

questions.prompt: What made HeLa cells scientifically significant?

They were used only to study diseases that affect the heart
They were created by combining human cells with plant cells
They were the first human cells to grow continuously in the laboratory

questions.prompt: In Moore v. Regents of the University of California (1990), the court held that:
choices: doctors may use patient tissue for profit and never need to tell patients anything
a hospital must destroy all tissue after the patient's treatment has ended
doctors must disclose research and financial interests, but the patient had no property right in the cells
a patient owns all of the cells that are ever removed from their body, in any medical or research context

Tissue samples always lose all of their scientific value once the first study has been completed
Donors have a legal property right in their samples under US federal law
Consent is never needed for research that does not involve a new procedure

To pay researchers and to decide which proposed studies will receive their funding
To publish the results of studies in scientific journals

Equal numbers of participants in each arm of every randomized trial

The ban on all kinds of genetic testing of people in the workplace

a somatic therapy that regulators had approved for a serious inherited blood disease in adults
